ety.text: Proto-Slavic *gunader. Late Latin gunna Old French gounebor. Middle English gowne English gown From Middle English gowne, from Anglo-Norman goune, gune (“fur-trimmed coat, pelisse”), from Old French goune, from Late Latin gunna (“leather garment, a fur”). Cognate with Manx gooyn, Irish gúna.

senses.d: A woman's ordinary outer dress, such as a calico or silk gown.
The official robe of certain professionals, clerics, and scholars, such as university students and officers, barristers, judges, etc.
ex:
VVhat is he an honeſt man? the deuill he is, he is the Parſon of the Towne,
You thinke ther’s no knauerie hid vnder a black gowne, […]

senses.d: The dress of civil officers, as opposed to military officers.
The university community, especially as contrasted with the local populace.
ex: In the perennial town versus gown battles, townies win some violent battles, but the collegians are winning the war.

senses.d: A loose wrapper worn by gentlemen within doors; a dressing gown.
Any sort of dress or garb.
The robe worn by a surgeon.
To dress in a gown, to don or garb with a gown.

ety.text: Inherited from Late Latin mantum, back-formation from mantellum, ultimately from Gaulish [Term?].

es:capa.gl: cloak, cape (a sleeveless garment hanging from the neck)

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish capa, from Late Latin cappa. Cognate with English cape and cope (“priestly vestment”). Compare English coping (“top layer of a brick wall”) for an English comparable semantic sense of a "layer".
Inherited from Old French, from Proto-Germanic *raubō (“booty”), later "stolen clothing".

chain.g: tunic, an undergarment worn by both men and women

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin tunica. Compare the inherited tonaca.

pt:vestido.gl: dress (woman’s garment which covers the upper part of the body as well as below the waist)

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese vestido, from Latin vestītus (“dressed; clothing”), perfect passive participle of vestiō (“to dress”), from vestis (“clothes”).
From Middle French togue, from Latin toga.
Proto-Indo-European *(s)teg-der. Proto-Italic *togā Latin togabor. Spanish toga Borrowed from Latin toga.
From tala, a tree species, from Quechua tara.
